answers.application: A: The whole is the complete 12-centimetre ribbon, and 6 and 6 are equal lengths, so one selected piece is 1/2. B: The whole is the complete 12-centimetre ribbon, and 3 and 9 are unequal lengths, so the pieces are not equal shares. C: The whole is the complete rectangular tray, and its four sections have equal areas, so one selected section is 1/4. D: The whole is the complete rectangular tray, and half, one quarter and one quarter are unequal amounts, so these three pieces are not equal thirds. E: The whole is the complete 15-centimetre ribbon, and 5, 5 and 5 are equal lengths, so one selected piece is 1/3. The selected piece in A is longer because it is 6 centimetres, while the selected piece in E is 5 centimetres. The whole ribbons have different lengths, so fraction labels alone are not enough to compare their actual selected lengths.
answers.teachBack: I first identify the complete object or amount being shared, such as the entire ribbon or the entire tray. Equal shares must contain the same amount, which means comparing lengths for a ribbon or areas for a flat tray. I would not agree that four pieces automatically make quarters, because I must check that all four pieces contain the same amount of that whole. Counting pieces without checking their sizes is insufficient.

answers.application:
name = "Alex"
tickets = 3
print(name)

Predicted output:
Alex
answers.teachBack: A variable name is the identifier used to find a stored value, so name identifies the variable while Alex is the text value it currently holds. Quotation marks tell Python that Alex is literal text, rather than another variable identifier. print(name) reads the value stored under name, so it displays Alex without quotation marks rather than displaying the letters name.

criteria.feedback: You correctly assign the text and number on separate lines.

answers.application:
A asks me to enter personal details through a supplied link under a deadline. That combination is suspicious, but the wording alone cannot prove who sent it. I would not open the link or provide details, and if checking is necessary I would contact the library using a known website or independently found phone number. I would use the email phishing-report control before deleting it.
B asks me to note a changed gardening-meeting time, with no reply or personal information required. It looks routine from its content, so I would note Saturday morning without sending information, while recognising that the text alone does not verify sender identity.
C asks me to open an attachment and send personal information immediately. Those requested actions and urgency are suspicious. I would not open the attachment or send details, and I would contact the volunteer organisation independently through a known contact if verification is needed. I would report it through the email phishing-report control before deleting it.
answers.teachBack: Identifying the requested action helps me see what the sender wants me to do and what I might expose. Urgent pressure and requests for personal information are reasons to pause, but urgency alone does not prove deception because a genuine notice might also be urgent. I would avoid supplied links and attachments, verify through a separate known contact when necessary, and report a suspicious message before deletion. I reject the idea that familiar branding proves safety, because anyone might copy a logo.

criteria.feedback: You correctly identify all three requests, including A’s linked personal-details request, B’s changed meeting time, and C’s attachment and information request.
